subject: humanities
passage: Shakespeare's sonnets reached print in 1609 in an edition issued by the publisher Thomas Thorpe, who also wrote its cryptic dedication. Nothing suggests the poet took part. A decade earlier, a contemporary had described the sonnets circulating in manuscript "among his private friends," and scholar Lucia Ferrante argues that Thorpe's edition most likely reflects the order in which he gathered such copies. Readers who trace a story across the sequence, she warns, are reading a design that may be the publisher's accident rather than the poet's intention.
passage_b: Whatever Thorpe's role, the 1609 arrangement displays more shape than accident can account for. The opening seventeen sonnets, all urging a young man to marry, form an unmistakable block; the one hundred twenty-sixth, with twelve lines instead of fourteen, reads as a deliberate farewell before the sequence turns to a very different addressee; linked pairs and echoed images run through the whole. An unauthorized edition is not the same thing as a random one. Some ordering hand, and plausibly the poet's, was at work before the copies reached the printer.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the warning issued by Ferrante in Text 1?

choices.A: By denying that the sonnets circulated in manuscript before 1609
choices.B: By granting that the edition may be unauthorized while arguing that its order is nonetheless deliberate
choices.C: By agreeing that the sequence reflects only the order in which Thorpe obtained the poems
choices.D: By insisting that Shakespeare himself prepared the 1609 edition for publication

explanation.why: Ferrante warns that the 1609 order may be the publisher's accident. Text 2 begins "Whatever Thorpe's role" and states that "an unauthorized edition is not the same thing as a random one," citing the marriage block, the twelve-line sonnet 126, and linked pairs as evidence of design. So the author of Text 2 sets aside the question of authorization and disputes the claim of accident.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 refers to "the copies" reaching the printer and never disputes manuscript circulation.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 concedes the edition may be unauthorized but argues from its internal structure that the order was deliberate.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 argues the opposite, that the order shows deliberate shape.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says only that "some ordering hand, and plausibly the poet's," was at work; it does not claim the poet prepared the edition.
